subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of likely reactions [Thinking]
passage:
Disha: You're the man who practised the bad-news call in the mirror, right?

Vaibhav: Ha, near enough. The night before, I sat with a notebook and imagined three clients. One furious: "This is unacceptable!" My reply: "You're right to be upset. Here's what happened and what we're doing." One asking whose fault it was: "I won't point at names. What matters is the date and the fix." One asking for a discount: "I can't decide that on this call. I'll raise it with my director and answer tomorrow." Writing them down stopped my stomach lurching. On the actual call the client was annoyed and did ask about a discount, and I already had my sentence. I didn't promise anything I couldn't keep.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav plan to say if the client asked for a discount?
qa.a: Vaibhav planned to say, "I can't decide that on this call. I'll raise it with my director and answer tomorrow."

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel before the replies were written down?
qa.a: Vaibhav was nervous, with a lurching stomach, until writing the replies calmed the nerves.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav do to prepare, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could practise the replies aloud with a colleague, because hearing them said out loud shows which words sound harsh or unclear.

qa.q: How might the client have felt on the call?
qa.a: The client was probably annoyed but also reassured, since the answers were calm, honest and made no promises that could not be kept.

grounding: Illustrates imagining an angry client, a request to name a culprit and a request for a discount, and drafting calm honest replies for each.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of likely reactions [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Santosh, and I share a cabin with Arnab at the consulting firm. The evening before he had to tell a retail client their new inventory system would be a month late, I watched him prepare.
He didn't write the bad news. He wrote the reactions. On a notepad, three headings: "They're angry." "Whose fault is it?" "Can we get a discount?"
Under each, he wrote a reply and read it out quietly, testing it. "I understand this is frustrating. Here's exactly what caused it." Then, "The delay came from our testing of their old data. We should have flagged it sooner. I'm not going to blame anyone on your side." Then, "I can't agree to a discount on this call, but I'll take it to my director today and come back to you by Friday."
He practised until his voice stayed level. I don't know how nervous he was inside, but the next morning, on the call, he never promised anything he couldn't keep.

qa.q: What were the three headings on Arnab's notepad?
qa.a: 'They're angry', 'Whose fault is it?' and 'Can we get a discount?'

qa.q: What might Arnab have been feeling the evening before the call?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about the client's reaction, practising until his voice stayed level.

qa.q: What else could Arnab do to prepare for reactions he didn't expect?
qa.a: He could keep a general reply ready, like 'Let me check and come back to you by a set time', so he isn't pushed into rash promises.

qa.q: How does Arnab's preparation look to Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh sees careful rehearsal and notices Arnab never promised anything he couldn't keep, though Santosh can't know how nervous Arnab felt.

grounding: Shows a person imagining a client's anger, blame and discount requests and drafting calm, honest replies for each so he isn't pushed into rash promises.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of likely reactions [Thinking]
passage:
Monday night. Ojas had to tell the logistics client on Wednesday that the tracking app would be six weeks late. He lay awake imagining the call. What if they shout? What if they ask who messed up? What if they demand money back?
Tuesday. He sat with his colleague Nirmala in the break room and rehearsed. "Pretend you're the client. Be angry."
Nirmala crossed her arms. "This is unacceptable! Who's responsible?"
Ojas took a breath. "I understand. The delay is on our side: the route data was more complex than we planned. I won't pretend otherwise."
"We want a discount."
"I can't decide that on this call. I'll speak to my manager and reply by Friday."
They did it three more times, harder each round.
Wednesday. The client was angry, and did ask for a discount. Ojas answered with the words he'd practised. He didn't promise anything he couldn't keep. The client ended with, "Fine. Friday, then."

qa.q: By when did Ojas promise to reply about the discount?
qa.a: He promised to reply by Friday.

qa.q: How was Ojas feeling on Monday night?
qa.a: He was anxious, lying awake imagining the client shouting, blaming and demanding money back.

qa.q: What else could Ojas do before the Friday reply?
qa.a: He could speak to his manager early and prepare a clear answer on the discount, so Friday's reply is firm and honest.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel playing the angry client?
qa.a: Nirmala may have found it a little fun, but also felt useful, helping Ojas stay calm by making each round harder.

grounding: Shows a person rehearsing a client's likely anger, blame and discount requests and preparing calm replies so he doesn't make rash promises.
